comment: I have few comment to add, It is really mesmerizing, but as you mentioned, there are definitely a few drawbacks. The movie is visually impressive overall, but some details could have been handled much better: In the initial war sequence of Indra vs. the Asuras, some objects seem to be missing proper shadows, which makes the CGI feel less realistic. The voice intensity of some characters doesn't always match their body language, which takes away from the impact of certain scenes. Lanka looks too dark and black-heavy, even with all the gold. I feel the visual design could have had more depth and contrast. The CGI quality noticeably drops in the scenes involving Kumbhakarna, as well as during the fight between Ravana and Vidyujjihva. These sequences feel much less polished compared to the overall visual quality of the movie. The lip-sync of the Rakshasi in the opening scene with young Dasana is really poor and immediately stands out. One detail that bothered me was the divine quivers given by Sage Agastya. They are supposed to ensure that Ram never runs out of arrows. In one scene, we actually see an arrow appear through CGI when he reaches for it, which was a great detail. But afterward, that effect completely disappears, and we can clearly see Ram's quiver looking empty in several shots. For a movie operating on this visual scale, I expected better consistency in those smaller details. Amazing experience overall, but definitely not peak attention to detail. As you said, hope they will improve in Part-2.

BUT, when it comes to Ravana's character writing, I personally feel it was completely inaccurate. Ravana was undoubtedly talented, highly knowledgeable, intelligent, and powerful, but that doesn't make him a good person. He was arrogant, immoral, and ultimately a symbol of evil. His character shouldn't be glorified or portrayed as a noble man just because of his knowledge and abilities. Ravana's Treatment of Women – References from the Ramayana 1. Ravana abducted women from the kingdoms he conquered.** **Uttara Kanda, Sarga 24, Shloka 1** Whenever Ravana returned from his conquests, he abducted the daughters of kings, sages, gods and Gandharvas and brought them with him. 2. Ravana killed the relatives of women he found attractive and imprisoned those women.** **Uttara Kanda, Sarga 24, Shloka 2** Whenever Ravana saw an attractive woman, he would kill her family members and relatives before imprisoning her in his flying chariot. 3. Hundreds of abducted women cried in captivity.** **Uttara Kanda, Sarga 24, Shloka 6** Hundreds of abducted women belonging to the Naga, Gandharva, sage, Daitya and Danava families were crying inside Ravana's flying chariot. 4. The abducted women condemned Ravana for pursuing other men's wives.** **Uttara Kanda, Sarga 24, Shloka 20** The women condemned Ravana's disgraceful behaviour, accusing him of pursuing and enjoying relationships with women who belonged to other men. 5. Ravana forcibly sexually assaulted Rambha, the intended wife of his nephew Nalakubera.** **Uttara Kanda, Sarga 26, Shloka 42** Overcome by lust, Ravana forced Rambha onto a rock and attempted to have sexual relations with her against her will. 7. Rambha told Nalakubera that Ravana ignored her pleas and forcibly violated her.** **Uttara Kanda, Sarga 26, Shloka 51** Rambha explained that she repeatedly begged Ravana to stop, reminding him that she was like his daughter-in-law. However, he ignored her pleas and forcibly violated her. 8. Nalakubera cursed Ravana for violating an unwilling woman.** **Uttara Kanda, Sarga 26, Shloka 57** Nalakubera cursed Ravana, declaring that if he ever tried to sexually force himself upon another unwilling woman, his head would split into seven pieces. This curse is significant because it explains why Ravana could not force himself physically upon Sita despite his repeated attempts to make her submit. 9. Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 13, Shlokas 11–15 Ravana had previously sexually assaulted Punjikasthala. comment: WHEN RAVANA BECOMES THE HERO AND BHAGAWAN RAMA THE VILLAIN… I watched the new Bollywood Ramayana, and honestly, I am outraged. Deeply, profoundly outraged. As an unapologetic Hindu, I find what has been done to the Ramayana absolutely unacceptable. There is a limit to artistic freedom, and there is a difference between creative interpretation and systematically distorting one of the most sacred Itihasas of Bharat. Why is Bollywood so desperately trying to whitewash Ravanasura? Why is Ravana being presented as a feminist, a kind-hearted ruler, a misunderstood intellectual and almost a noble hero? Why are his atrocities being conveniently pushed into the background while his character is glorified? Are we supposed to forget who Ravana was? According to the Ramayana tradition, Ravana was not merely a learned scholar or a devotee of Shiva. He was also an immensely arrogant, lustful, cruel and tyrannical ruler. His knowledge did not make him righteous. His devotion did not absolve his crimes. His greatness in certain accomplishments did not erase the darkness of his character. He abducted another man’s wife. He violated the dignity of women. He imprisoned women and kept numerous women in his palace against their will. His conduct towards Rambha is also described in the Ramayana tradition. This is the man whose character is now being polished to make him attractive to modern audiences? And what about the consequences of his arrogance? He dragged his entire kingdom into a catastrophic war. His own sons, brothers and countless warriors perished. He knew the danger of awakening Kumbhakarna from his sleep, yet even his brother was drawn into this disastrous war. His obsession with Sita ultimately destroyed his family and his kingdom. Is this the character we are supposed to admire? And then there is Surpanakha. In Valmiki Ramayana, her appearance is described very differently from the conventionally beautiful portrayal in this film. More importantly, her actions and intentions are essential to understanding the events that followed. Instead, the film seems determined to turn the Rakshasa characters into victims and portray the events almost entirely from their perspective. For the first hour, I felt as though I was watching a campaign to establish the moral superiority of the Rakshasas! Lakshmana is made to look cruel. Bhagawan Rama is portrayed as timid. Sita’s dialogues are deeply disappointing in several places. She even appears to scold Lakshmana over Surpanakha’s disfigurement and encourage Rama to pursue her. Is this how these characters should be represented? And what happened to the dignity and suffering of Mata Sita during her abduction? In Valmiki Ramayana, Ravana forcibly abducts Sita and takes her away against her will. Her anguish, her resistance, her helplessness and her extraordinary courage are central to this episode. Yet why dilute the brutality of that moment? Why soften the actions of the perpetrator? And Bhagawan Rama? Rama, who never abandoned his duty. Rama, who stood fearlessly before his enemies. Rama, whose courage, composure, compassion and righteousness became the very definition of ideal conduct. Why portray him as someone who runs away from Rakshasas? Why make him appear timid when his defining quality is extraordinary courage? The greatest tragedy is not simply that Ravana has been glorified. It is that, in the process, Bhagawan Rama appears to have been diminished. And this is what makes me particularly angry. Millions of Hindus grow up listening to the Ramayana. For generations, Bhagawan Rama has represented Maryada, Dharma, truth, courage, sacrifice, self-control and responsibility. He is Maryada Purushottama — the ideal human being. We want our children to watch the Ramayana and aspire to become like Rama. We want them to learn from his integrity, his devotion to duty, his respect for others, his courage in adversity and his unwavering commitment to Dharma. But what is this film teaching them? That the villain was actually misunderstood? That arrogance is greatness? That intellectual brilliance excuses cruelty? That abducting a woman can be romanticised? That the person who commits atrocities deserves more sympathy than the one who stands for Dharma? What exactly are we supposed to take home from this film — inspiration from Bhagawan Rama or admiration for Ravanasura? I have absolutely no objection to exploring the complexity of Ravana’s character. He was learned, powerful and a great Shiva devotee. These aspects are part of the tradition. But acknowledging his qualities does not require whitewashing his crimes. A character can be intellectually brilliant and morally corrupt. A person can possess extraordinary knowledge and still be consumed by Adharma. That is precisely one of the profound lessons of the Ramayana! Ravana’s downfall is not the downfall of an ordinary villain. It is the downfall of a man who possessed knowledge, power, wealth and extraordinary abilities but lacked the humility and self-control to live by Dharma. That is the lesson. Do not destroy the lesson in order to glorify the villain. Bollywood must understand that the Ramayana is not just another fictional story available for arbitrary character makeovers. It is the living civilisational heritage of millions of Hindus. It deserves research, responsibility, sensitivity and above all, respect. Creative freedom cannot become an excuse for civilisational distortion. You can make a film about Ravana. You can explore his psychology, his scholarship, his devotion and even his perspective. But do not expect Hindus to remain silent when Bhagawan Rama is diminished and Ravanasura is glorified. I am not asking filmmakers to make every character one-dimensional. I am asking them not to reverse the moral compass of the Ramayana. Rama must remain Rama. Dharma must remain Dharma. And Ravana’s Adharma must not be repackaged as virtue. After watching the Ramayana, people should leave the theatre wanting to follow the path of Bhagawan Rama — not aspiring to become Ravanasura. That is the whole point. Jai Shri Ram! 🙏 An unapologetic Hindu.

comment: Visually, Ramayana: Part 1 is a landmark for Indian cinema—the VFX is world-class, the landscapes feel massive, and Jatayu's CGI is incredible. Honestly, the spectacle alone carries the film. Unfortunately, the screenplay strips the epic of its soul. Instead of weaving parallel perspectives or inner conflict, it plods through a predictable sequence that offers zero tension for a story we already know. The biggest flaw, however, is whitewashing Ravana to cater to star-power metrics. Rather than showing how unchecked ego and lust corrupted a brilliant scholar into an arrogant tyrant, the film turns Devas vs. Asuras into a basic political power struggle and frames Ravana as a noble liberator. Rewriting Surpanakha’s husband’s death as self-defense, making Sita question Lakshmana to build sympathy for Ravana, and reducing his curse against violating women to a split-second flash completely manipulates the audience. They could have used his ten heads to show his wisdom losing to his arrogance before every wrong choice. Instead, by scrubbing away his evil to make him a tragic anti-hero, they hollowed out Rama’s purpose—downgrading a cosmic battle of Dharma vs. Adharma into a mere misunderstanding between warriors. Great fantasy spectacle, but calling it Ramayana feels unearned.

comment: I genuinely appreciate the effort the makers have put into exploring Ravana’s character and relationships. Almost every relationship gets some context, whether it’s his mother, brothers, sister, sister-in-law, Maricha, or even his moments with his multiple heads. However, when it comes to Lord Rama, the emotional depth feels quite limited. Apart from Rama, Sita and Lakshmana (whom I consider one emotional unit), we barely see his other relationships. There is just one conversation between Rama and Bharata, despite their extraordinary love, respect and devotion towards each other. Similarly, there isn’t even a meaningful conversation between Rama and his mother Kaushalya when he leaves for exile. Even Sumitra and Shatrughna deserved at least one dialogue. I feel the entire sequence involving Ravana’s sister-in-law and her husband could easily have been removed. The makers could have directly shown Surpanakha living with her brothers, Khara and Dushana, in Dandakaranya. This would have saved approximately 15–20 minutes, which could have been used to show Bharata’s anger towards Kaikeyi, his emotional breakdown and, most importantly, his devotion towards his elder brother. Sometimes it feels like the makers are more interested in showcasing Yash’s performance as Ravana and his action sequences than balancing the emotional depth of the story. A few things I sincerely hope the makers don’t miss in Part 2 and Part 3: * Rama and Shabari’s meeting – one of the most beautiful examples of devotion. * Bharata Milap and the extraordinary bond between the brothers. * Lakshmana’s unconsciousness and Rama’s emotional reaction. * The devotion of the Vanara Sena towards Rama. * Vibhishana’s surrender and devotion towards Lord Rama. * Hanuman ji’s pure devotion, humility and kindness towards Lord Rama. Talking about Hanuman ji, I know the makers will probably present him (played by Sunny Deol, who is known for his larger-than-life and aggressive screen presence) as an extremely powerful character, just as they have presented Ravana. But I sincerely hope they don’t focus only on his strength, aggression and action sequences. Hanuman ji’s real greatness lies not just in his extraordinary power, but in his humility, kindness and unconditional devotion towards Lord Rama. His first meeting with Rama and his dedication to serving him deserve just as much attention as his heroic battles. Coming to the music: I know music is subjective, but considering the criticism surrounding the current music and lyrics, I strongly feel A. R. Rahman and Kumar Vishwas should be replaced with more deserving talent for the next part. The music and lyrics need to match the emotional and devotional scale of this epic. Two storytelling concerns: 1. Ravana’s motivation: Traditionally, Ravana’s attraction and lust towards Sita play an important role in her abduction. However, the movie seems to change this motivation considerably. It gives the impression that Ravana abducted Sita mainly to provoke Rama, whom he believes to be Lord Vishnu, into fighting him. But if his objective was simply to fight Rama, why travel all the way from Lanka, abduct Sita and take her away in Pushpak Vimana? Why not directly challenge Rama? This could give first-time viewers a completely different understanding of Ravana’s character and his actual motivation. 2. Surpanakha’s episode: The movie almost makes it look as though the entire conflict happened because Lakshmana unnecessarily cut Surpanakha’s nose. Even Sita questions Lakshmana’s actions. However, Surpanakha’s own behaviour, her advances towards Rama and her attempts to deceive Rama through her disguise also needed proper context. Showing only one side makes the incident look quite different from how the audience might understand it through the traditional Ramayana. My biggest request to the makers: Today, social media trends seem to favour aggression, action, grey characters and larger-than-life performances over simple and pure emotions. But the Ramayana is not just an action story about Rama versus Ravana. It is a complete emotional journey of Lord Rama, his relationships, sacrifices, devotion, struggles and his battle against evil to establish righteousness. I want my child to watch this Ramayana and remember more than just its grand visuals, powerful characters and fight sequences. I want him to learn brotherhood from Rama and Bharata, sacrifice from Lakshmana, devotion from Hanuman ji and Shabari, and the importance of righteousness from the entire epic. The real success of this trilogy, for me, would be if our children walk away not just remembering how grand the movie was, but also carrying some of the beautiful values and lessons of the Ramayana into their lives. We don’t just want to see bigger battles and more action sequences. We also want to FEEL the Ramayana. That’s what will make this trilogy truly memorable.

Ravana was undoubtedly talented, highly knowledgeable, intelligent, and powerful, but that doesn't make him a good person. He was arrogant, immoral, and ultimately a symbol of evil. His character shouldn't be glorified or portrayed as a noble man just because of his knowledge and abilities. Ravana's Treatment of Women – References from the Ramayana 1. Ravana abducted women from the kingdoms he conquered.** **Uttara Kanda, Sarga 24, Shloka 1** Whenever Ravana returned from his conquests, he abducted the daughters of kings, sages, gods and Gandharvas and brought them with him. 2. comment: I just watched Ramayana in IMAX 3D, in Hindi, at a cinema in Paris. Overall, I enjoyed the film and would give it 3 out of 5 stars. I loved the visuals, the aesthetics, Raavan’s magnificent costumes, and the storyline. There is strong chemistry between Raavan and Sita on screen, but unfortunately, absolutely none between Sita and Ram. I found Ranbir Kapoor’s performance rather flat and bland. I felt no emotion whatsoever, whereas I still laugh and cry during certain scenes of Baahubali, even after watching it ten times! I honestly think the role of Ram should have gone to another actor with more charisma. The actors playing Raavan and Lakshman, on the other hand, are absolutely outstanding!

comment: "I watched the movie Ramayana in the theater just yesterday, and I am deeply disappointed that a movie was made on such a great epic like the Ramayana, only for it to look so artificial and duplicate. I honestly can’t understand what they spent ₹2,000 crores on! Maybe my perspective on watching movies is different, and perhaps other people enjoy that artificial feel, AI-generated videos, scenes, or heavy VFX. But I feel that whenever an audience watches any movie, it shouldn't feel fake or plastic. For instance, let’s talk about our own Indian cinema—take BaahuBali. Even in BaahuBali, massive battle scenes were shown, but they never felt fake or duplicate. However, while watching Ramayana, the scenes felt so extremely, overwhelmingly fake, and it honestly surprises me how no one is talking about this. Another point I’d like to mention is that I have watched Game of Thrones. The scenes, the visualization, how real it feels, and the goosebump-inducing moments—everything looks so grand and magnificent. If they spent a staggering ₹2,000 crores making the Ramayana movie and ended up creating such artificial scenes, I simply don’t understand where the ₹2,000 crores went! Whether I understand filmmaking deeply or not is a different question, but as a regular viewer and comparing it to other movies, I am utterly disappointed with this film."
